analysis.one_liner: Lets the U.S. Postal Service offer small loans, bank accounts, money transfers, and a prepaid card.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Oversight Committee after being referred there in July 2017, and it expired when that Congress ended with no vote ever taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let the post office provide basic banking: small-dollar loans, checking and interest-bearing savings accounts, international money transfers, and a 'Postal Card' prepaid card. Services could be offered by the Postal Service itself or in partnership with banks and credit unions. The idea is to give people without bank accounts — especially in areas where bank branches have closed — a public option for everyday finance at lower cost than payday lenders or check-cashing stores. The bill was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 9 million U.S. households without a bank account and millions more who rely on payday loans, check cashers, and high-fee money transfers would gain access to basic financial services at postal rates. Rural residents and lower-income neighborhoods hit by bank branch closures would be the biggest winners, since post offices remain in places banks have left.

how_it_helps.text: Amends federal postal law to add 'basic financial services' to the Postal Service's powers, including small-dollar loans, checking accounts, interest-bearing savings accounts, international money transfers, and other services it deems in the public interest.
Creates a 'Postal Card' prepaid card that lets users access those financial services at post offices.

Services may be provided by USPS alone or in partnership with FDIC-insured banks and credit unions, using post offices that already operate in thousands of communities, including areas banks have exited.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, check-cashing outlets, and remittance-transfer companies that charge high fees for the same services would lose customers if the post office offered cheaper alternatives. Banks and credit unions that profit from overdraft and account fees on lower-income customers could also see some competition, though the bill allows them to partner with USPS rather than compete with it.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no provisions on pricing, loan underwriting standards, interest rate caps for postal loans, or risk management, so the costs and safety of postal lending would depend entirely on future Postal Service decisions and additional rulemaking.

Critics of postal banking have long argued the Postal Service — already financially strained — could take on lending losses and regulatory burdens it is not equipped to manage, adding risk to a public agency that taxpayers ultimately back.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households living outside the banking system, the potential gains are concrete: small loans without triple-digit interest and account access without branch-closure deserts. The bill's main weakness is that it is an enabling measure only — it grants authority but sets no rate limits, pricing rules, or capital requirements, leaving the hardest questions unresolved. Whether the Postal Service could manage lending risk without new subsidies was a fair, open objection. On balance, the potential benefit to underserved households outweighs the manageable downside, but the bill's thinness made it more a statement of principle than a ready program.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again; when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019, it died with no hearing, no vote, and no Senate companion.

narrative.text: Rep. Cedric Richmond and five original cosponsors introduced the bill on July 28, 2017, to add basic financial services to the Postal Service's legal powers.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.
The bill attracted 17 cosponsors, all Democrats.
No further action was ever recorded: no committee markup, no report, no floor vote, and no companion bill in the Senate.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders, check-cashing outlets, and remittance companies kept their market for small-dollar credit and money transfers uncontested, since the only public competitor that could have offered cheaper services was never allowed to start. The Postal Service gained nothing, and unbanked households remained where they were.

for.name: Rep. Cedric L. Richmond
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let USPS offer small-dollar loans, bank accounts, money transfers, and a prepaid card.

for.name: Reps. Grijalva, Conyers, Kaptur, Blumenauer, and Rush
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jason Chaffetz (R-UT) until mid-2017
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

against.name: Payday lending and check-cashing industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed postal banking proposals that would let the Postal Service offer small loans and money transfers at lower prices than their own products.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats; the bill received no Republican cosponsors and no committee action in a Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: Postal small-dollar loans would have competed directly with payday loans that often carry triple-digit annual rates. Their interest in the bill ran against the unbanked customers who would have gained a cheaper option.

Postal money-transfer services and a prepaid card would undercut the fees these companies charge for cashing checks and sending money abroad. Their fees are typically highest in exactly the neighborhoods the bill aimed to serve.

The bill lets banks and credit unions partner with USPS to deliver accounts and transfers, which could bring them new customers; but a postal alternative also threatens overdraft and account-fee revenue from lower-income customers.

The bill would have given USPS a new revenue line at a time of financial pressure, using its existing retail network. Its gain ran alongside the public's, since the same post offices would deliver the services.
